verses.text: The enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned exiles were building a temple for the LORD, the God of Israel.
They approached Zerubbabel and the family heads and said, "Let us build with you. We seek your God just as you do. We've been sacrificing to him since King Esar Haddon of Assyria brought us here."

Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the other heads of Israel's families answered, "You have no share in building a house for our God. We'll build it ourselves for the LORD, the God of Israel, as King Cyrus of Persia commanded us."
Then the people of the land discouraged the people of Judah and made it difficult for them to build.
They hired advisers to work against them and block their plans throughout the reign of King Cyrus of Persia and into the reign of King Darius of Persia.
At the beginning of Ahasuerus's reign, they wrote an accusation against the people of Judah and Jerusalem.
In Artaxerxes' time, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and their associates wrote to King Artaxerxes of Persia. The letter was written in Aramaic script and delivered in the Aramaic language.
Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the secretary wrote a letter against Jerusalem to King Artaxerxes, as follows.
It came from Rehum the chancellor, Shimshai the secretary, and their associates: the Dinaites, Apharsathchites, Tarpelites, Apharsites, Archevites, Babylonians, Shushanchites, Dehaites, and Elamites,
and the other peoples whom the great and noble Osnappar had moved and settled in Samaria and elsewhere in the province Beyond the River.
This is a copy of the letter they sent: "To King Artaxerxes, from your servants in the province Beyond the River.
Let the king know that the Jews who left your territory have come to Jerusalem. They're rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They've finished its walls and repaired its foundations.
Let the king also know that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are finished, the people will stop paying tribute, customs, and tolls. In the end the kings will lose revenue.
Since we owe our living to the palace, we can't stand by and watch the king be dishonored. So we're writing to inform you

and ask that you search your ancestors' records. You'll find that this city has a history of rebellion and has brought trouble to kings and provinces. People have stirred up revolts there before. That's why the city was destroyed.
We warn the king that if this city is rebuilt and the walls are finished, you'll lose control of the province Beyond the River."
Then the king replied: "To Rehum the chancellor, Shimshai the secretary, and their associates living in Samaria and elsewhere in the province Beyond the River. Peace.
The letter you sent us has been read aloud clearly to me.
I ordered a search, and it confirmed that this city has risen against kings before and has been the site of rebellion and revolt.
Powerful kings have ruled from Jerusalem over the whole province Beyond the River, and they received tribute, customs, and tolls.
Issue an order now to stop these men. The city must stay as it is until I issue another decree.
See that you do this promptly. Why let the damage grow and harm the kings?"
As soon as a copy of King Artaxerxes' letter was read to Rehum, Shimshai the secretary, and their associates, they hurried to the Jews in Jerusalem and forced them to stop.
Then work on God's house in Jerusalem came to a halt. It remained stopped until the second year of King Darius of Persia.
